item.title: Cognizant sets up Claude Frontier group with over 25,000 professionals
item.description: The IT services firm also introduces a managed services model for Claude, aiming to help enterprises deploy, operate and scale AI systems securely across core business functions ...
item.dc:creator: Our Bureau
item.content:encoded: Cognizant on Tuesday announced the formation of the Claude Frontier Capability Group, with more than 25,000 professionals committed to delivering Claude for clients. The group is focused on execution, transformation and client success, with the scale to take AI from pilot to production across enterprises’ core operations, the company said in a press statement. Cognizant is also introducing a managed services model for Claude. Under the model, Cognizant manages the operation of Claude-powered systems in production on clients’ behalf so they can focus on the business results it makes possible. Both initiatives draw on Cognizant’s Frontier workforce model, through which it is developing Frontier Certified Engineers and Frontier Business Operators credentialled directly by frontier-model companies. Enterprises have access to frontier AI capabilities but continue to face challenges in delivering value to their businesses. Cognizant has built Claude skills throughout its workforce, with more than 44,000 associates in business units and corporate functions already trained or certified on Claude. The new group is a dedicated organisation building and running Claude-powered systems inside client businesses. “Clients want a partner who will take responsibility for delivery once AI is running inside their business,” said Ravi Kumar S, CEO of Cognizant. “We are putting more than 25,000 of our people on Claude and taking on the job of running it for clients through managed services. That is a significant bet on Claude, and on what enterprises can achieve with it in their core operations.” Cognizant’s managed services model supports the operation of Claude in production for clients, combining dedicated talent, licensed access to Claude and Cognizant’s own IP, including its AI Delivery Operating System. The model gives clients more predictable AI spending and runs every engagement within enterprise-grade security and governance controls, customised to each client’s connectivity, architecture and risk requirements. “Every enterprise is racing to bring AI into its organization, but the people with the skills to make it work inside a real business have become the hardest talent to find,” said Paul Smith, chief commercial officer, Anthropic. “Cognizant is working to address that gap, committing more than 25,000 people to help their customers put Claude to work across their businesses.” The group will initially focus on four areas: redesigning business domains around AI, building and modernising the systems that support them, operating agents securely at scale and establishing AI-native software engineering as a core delivery capability. Cognizant holds more than 26,000 Claude certifications and ranks first globally for Claude Certified Architect: Foundations. The company is deploying Claude across its workforce, including corporate functions, engineering and delivery teams, as announced in November 2025.

item.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with faster AI capabilities
item.description: Anthropic says its latest AI models offer faster responses and stronger coding, reasoning and research capabilities, while Fable 5.2 comes with lower pricing and safeguards ...
item.dc:creator: Vrinda Goel
item.content:encoded: Anthropic on Monday announced the launch of its latest and most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. The company says these models offer significant improvements in coding, reasoning and visual tasks, along with clearer communication. The upgraded models can generate outputs up to 30 per cent faster than their predecessors, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. Anthropic has also reduced Fable's pricing from $10 to $8 per million input tokens, making Fable 5.2 cheaper than its primary competitor, GPT-6 Astra. What can Anthropic's Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 do? Anthropic said Fable 5.2 can handle more complex software engineering work, hardware-related tasks such as controlling robots, and long-running projects. It is also designed to coordinate more than 1,000 AI agents simultaneously. The company said early testers found that the new models communicate more clearly than previous Fable and Mythos versions. They also showed better judgement on ambiguous, data-heavy research and analysis tasks, particularly those involving abstract reasoning and design. Fable 5.2 can function as an adviser, with smaller models such as Haiku, Sonnet or Opus consulting it to solve difficult problems. It can also act as an orchestrator, delegating simpler tasks to smaller models. Anthropic recommends that users begin with Claude Opus 5.5, which it describes as its strongest everyday model, for most coding and knowledge-based tasks. They can then move to Fable or Mythos for more complex work, or use Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 for less demanding tasks. Mythos 5.2 is being made available to select organisations and is described by Anthropic as its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. The company says it can identify more vulnerabilities than earlier models and is better at reproducing and fixing them. Fable 5.2, meanwhile, has safeguards that block most cybersecurity-related tasks. Safety testing Anthropic said it conducted extensive pre-release safety testing on the model underlying both releases. The company said high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low and that the model performed as well as, or better than, recent versions on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2's cybersecurity and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1, while producing fewer unnecessary blocks. Anthropic also said it had introduced its strongest protections yet against distillation attacks. Where are Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 available? Claude Fable 5.2 is available across platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Anthropic is also offering eligible paid subscribers additional usage this week. Subscribers on plans and seats that include Fable models will receive one to three usage resets, depending on how long they have subscribed. Fable will also be included for up to 50 per cent of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Mythos 5.2 through Anthropic's Cyber Verification Programme. Fast mode for both models is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (both Anthropic-managed and Google-managed) and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic-hosted). Access to Mythos 5.2's fast mode is restricted to organisations participating in Anthropic's verification programmes.

item.title: Higher financing costs to weaken global credit conditions in 2027: Moody's
item.description: Moody's Ratings expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 as higher financing costs and energy prices strain borrowers, while AI investments and policy shifts reshape markets ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Higher financing costs to weaken global credit conditions in 2027: Moody's

Higher financing costs to weaken global credit conditions in 2027: Moody's Moody's Ratings expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 as higher financing costs and energy prices strain borrowers, while AI investments and policy shifts reshape markets

(Photo: Reuters)

Press Trust of India New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 4:36 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Moody's Ratings on Tuesday said it expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 due to higher financing costs and elevated energy prices. The Moody's Ratings' 2027 Global Credit Conditions Outlook report examines the key forces that could shape credit markets in the year ahead. It said AI investment will remain massive, but investors will increasingly focus on whether revenues and productivity gains justify the scale of spending. "Business model disruption will become more visible: some companies will gain from stronger demand and productivity, while others face more competition and weaker pricing power," Moody's Ratings said. Besides, Moody's expects government intervention through tariffs, regulation, export controls and strategic investment to play a growing role in credit outcomes.

"As many of these tools can be introduced or reversed by executive action, policy can shift quickly, therefore this will continue to influence trade, capital allocation and competition in 2027," it added. Rising spending on energy security, critical minerals, defence, and climate resilience will create opportunities for some sectors while increasing costs for others. Also, higher refinancing costs will put greater pressure on highly leveraged issuers and borrowers with significant near-term maturities. "Moody's Ratings expects global credit conditions to weaken in 2027 as higher financing costs and elevated energy prices create pockets of pressure, even as major economies continue to expand," the agency said.

item.title: US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review
item.description: The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review

US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review Trump administration declines to participate in the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, which examines the rights records of all 193 member states every four to five years

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago | Image: Bloomberg

AP Geneva 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 2:47 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the US out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-US and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all UN member states including the US, which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific - which the administration has said are designed to protect US workers and help keep the country safe.

The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 UN member states - generally about every four to five years - as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the US government might change its mind. Also Read

Bangladesh's troubled history and questions about its political future

US visa curbs: Will Indian IT firms shift more technology work offshore?

Meet Nithya Raman, the India-born politician who won LA mayoral race

US AI data centres turn to retired jet engines to meet power demand

Private jet carrying 9 crashes near Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida

It did not. "(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council's "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."   The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies. Critics of the US snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit. Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed'."   "And we are saying: No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable'," he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the US rights record.

He said the ACLU and allies have called on the UN human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year. Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system. "If the predominant global power - which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms - doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.
